after: ## The six levels in the specification
alt: A table of the six levels in the specification: phonetics, phonology and prosodics; graphology; lexis and semantics; grammar including morphology; pragmatics; and discourse. Each is shown with its specification wording and what it gives you when analysing Paper 1 texts.
caption: Six levels, each giving you a different kind of evidence about a text.

alt: A decision flow: ask whether changing a feature would change the representation or relationship. If yes, it is salient and worth analysing; if no, leave it out. Repeated patterns and marked choices are usually more salient than isolated features.
caption: Salient means prominent and significant: the features that do most to create the text's meanings.

after: ## Level by level: the terminology that earns credit
alt: Four ranks of grammar from word up to sentence. Word: word classes and morphology. Phrase: noun phrase structure and verb phrase tense, aspect, modality and voice. Clause: clause elements, main and subordinate clauses and fronted adverbials. Sentence: the four functions and five structures.
caption: Describe grammar at word, phrase, clause and sentence level, working upwards.

after: ## Worked example: describing salient features precisely
alt: The lesson's original café leaflet is split into its five sentences, each linked to a salient feature: opening and closing imperatives with domestic, informal lexis, an implied welcome for newcomers, a tricolon of parallel clauses with "our", and a presupposition that the reader will visit. A bracket shows the circular invitation, reasons, invitation structure.
caption: Name the structure, quote it and state the meaning it helps create.

alt: The sentence "The tired volunteers who had worked all night finally closed the doors" is split into chips. The noun phrase is labelled determiner, pre-modifier, head and post-modifying relative clause; "finally" is an adverbial and "closed" a simple past main verb, with "had worked" in the past perfect. A note replaces "a long sentence" with a precise description.
caption: Accurate grammatical description lets you make a confident claim about meaning.

after: ## Applying methods to children's data (Section B)
alt: Five levels applied to children's data: phonological processes such as substitution, deletion and reduplication; over- and underextension; inflections, negatives and questions; turn-taking and politeness; and graphology and orthography in writing. All feed into describing the data first, with theory following.
caption: Describe the child's language level by level first; bring in theory after.

alt: Three stepped stages using the lesson's grammar example: identify names the feature (a relative clause), describe says how it is formed (a post-modifying relative clause in the noun phrase), and analyse explains its meaning (it delays the verb so effort is foregrounded). A note advises planning by meaning before choosing levels.
caption: Paper 1 analysis needs all three steps, not just a feature name.
